props.title: Making Mr. Right

sections.content: Making Mr. Right sits at a fascinating intersection of 80s romantic comedy and sci-fi, following the path carved by Weird Science (1985) but with a distinctly feminist twist. Director Susan Seidelman, fresh off her success with Desperately Seeking Susan (1985), brings her signature New Wave sensibility to this tale of a PR specialist hired to humanize an android. The film cleverly subverts expectations by having Ann Magnuson play both the career woman Frankie Stone and the android's creator, Dr. Jeff Peters, while John Malkovich delivers a remarkably nuanced dual performance as both the emotionally stunted scientist and his creation Ulysses.

sections.content: The film emerges from a specific moment in 80s cinema when technology narratives were becoming more intimate and domestic, rather than purely threatening. Like Blade Runner (1982), it explores the potential for machines to develop genuine emotions, but does so through the lens of romantic comedy rather than noir. This approach aligns it with films like Earth Girls Are Easy (1988) and My Stepmother is an Alien (1988), which use sci-fi elements to examine gender roles and relationships.

Seidelman's direction brings a distinct visual style that bridges the slick corporate world of 80s Miami with retro-futuristic laboratory settings. The film's aesthetic shares DNA with other contemporary sci-fi comedies like Real Genius (1985) and Innerspace (1987), but its examination of artificial intelligence and human emotion feels surprisingly prescient, predating similar themes in films like A.I. sections.content: Making Mr. Right marked an important shift in how Hollywood portrayed human-android relationships. Unlike the threatening artificial beings in The Terminator (1984) or the subservient robots in Rocky IV (1985), Ulysses represents a more complex exploration of artificial consciousness. This paved the way for later films like Bicentennial Man (1999) and Ex Machina (2014), which further developed the concept of machines developing genuine emotional connections.
